Part 1 of 6

The Rise of Fascism

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 1: Explain what gave rise to fascism and assess how authoritarian leaders were able to gain control in Germany, Italy, Spain, and Japan.

IN MY WORDS: In your own words, what is fascism, and how did dictators take power?

Reading AWhat Was Fascism?

Fascism was a Far-Right form of government in which a dictator gained power and popularity through emotional appeals to nationalism and by demonizing political enemies, the press, and other groups. Fascists used brute force to seize control of all aspects of national life—the economy, armed forces, legal and educational systems, and media. . . . In Germany, the movement built on claims of racial superiority and the simmering resentments that grew out of that nation’s defeat in the Great War.

Word help: Far-Right = the extreme side of politics that wants a strong leader and one nation · dictator = a ruler with total power · nationalism = extreme pride in your nation · demonizing = making people look evil · brute force = violence · resentments = angry feelings

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 24, “The Rise of Fascism in Europe” (p. 1050).

Reading BMussolini and Hitler

In 1922, Benito Mussolini and 40,000 of his black-shirted fascist supporters seized control of Italy, taking advantage of an inept government incapable of dealing with widespread unemployment, runaway inflation, mass strikes, and fears of communism. . . . He frequently ordered the murder of political rivals and eliminated all political parties except the Fascists.

The objective of fascism was to replace diversity with unity: “one people, one state, one leader,” in the Nazi slogan. Hitler and the Nazis claimed to represent a German master race whose “purity and strength” were threatened by liberals, Communists, and other “inferior” peoples: Jews, socialists, Romani, and homosexuals.

Hitler was appointed chancellor of Germany on January 30, 1933 . . . Like Mussolini, Hitler quickly declared himself absolute leader, or Führer; stripped political enemies of their voting and civil rights; and created a secret police force known as the Gestapo.

Word help: inept = not able to do the job · runaway inflation = prices rising very fast · rivals = opponents · master race = the false idea that one group is better than all others · chancellor = head of the German government · secret police = police who spy on and arrest critics

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 24, “The Rise of Fascism in Europe” (Italy and Germany) (p. 1050).

Reading CAggression Spreads

In 1931–1932, some 10,000 Japanese troops occupied northeast China’s province of Manchuria—a territory rich in raw materials; mineral deposits, including iron ore and coal; and farmland.

In 1935, in flagrant violation of the Treaty of Versailles, Adolf Hitler began rebuilding Germany’s armed forces. . . . The unwillingness of France and Great Britain to counter Hitler’s aggressive moves convinced Hitler that the western democracies were cowards.

The year 1936 also witnessed the outbreak of the Spanish Civil War, which began when Spanish troops (the Nationalists) loyal to General Francisco Franco, with the support of the Roman Catholic Church, revolted against the fragile new democratic government . . . The fall of the Spanish Republic in March 1939 resulted in another dictatorial regime in Europe, this one led by Franco.

Word help: occupied = took over with soldiers · flagrant violation = openly breaking · Treaty of Versailles = the peace treaty that ended World War I · counter = push back against · revolted = rose up against

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 24, “The Rise of Fascism in Europe” (Expanding Aggression) (p. 1052).

Part 2 of 6

From Neutrality to War

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 2: Evaluate how President Franklin Roosevelt and Congress responded to the events leading to the outbreak and early stages of wars in Europe and Asia between 1933 and 1941.

IN MY WORDS: How did the United States go from staying out of the war to fighting in it?

Reading DNeutrality Laws and the Axis

Most Americans responded to the mounting world crises by deepening their commitment to isolationism. . . . Such strongly felt isolationism led President Roosevelt to sign the first of several “neutrality laws” to help avoid U.S. involvement in another war.

The Neutrality Act of 1935 prohibited American manufacturers from selling weapons to nations at war (“belligerents”) and banned citizens from traveling on ships owned by belligerents.

In 1937, Japan joined Germany and Italy in establishing the Rome-Berlin-Tokyo Axis alliance . . . “Because of its neutrality laws,” he said, “America is not dangerous to us.”

Word help: isolationism = staying out of other nations’ wars and problems · neutrality = not taking sides · prohibited = did not allow · belligerents = nations at war · alliance = a group of nations that agree to help each other · he = Adolf Hitler

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 24, “From Isolationism to Intervention” (U.S. Neutrality; The Axis Alliance) (p. 1054).

Reading ELightning War

On September 1, 1939, just nine days after the German government announced the alliance with Stalin, 1.5 million German troops invaded Poland from the north, south, and west. . . . On September 3, Great Britain and France declared war against Germany as Americans watched in horror.

Hitler’s blitzkrieg (“lightning war”) strategy centered on speed. Columns of tanks, motorized artillery, and truck-borne infantry, supported by warplanes and paratroopers, moved so fast they stunned their opponents.

Eight days later, French leaders officially surrendered . . . In the United States, complacency turned to fear and even panic as people realized that the Germans, who now ruled most of western Europe, could eventually assault America. Great Britain stood alone against Hitler’s military power.

Word help: invaded = attacked and entered · artillery = big guns · infantry = foot soldiers · paratroopers = soldiers who jump from planes · complacency = feeling safe and not worried · assault = attack

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 24, “From Isolationism to Intervention” (The Conquest of Poland; “Phony War” in Europe) (p. 1055).

Reading FLend-Lease and the Atlantic Charter

The Lend-Lease Act (officially “An Act to Promote the Defense of the United States”), introduced in Congress on January 10, 1941, allowed the president to lend or lease military equipment to “any country whose defense the President deems vital to the defense of the United States.” . . . “We must be the great arsenal of democracy,” Roosevelt explained.

In August 1941, Roosevelt and Churchill met on a warship off the Canadian coast and drew up a joint statement of “common principles” known as the Atlantic Charter. The agreement pledged that after the “final destruction of the Nazi tyranny,” the victors would promote the self-determination of all peoples, economic cooperation, freedom of the seas, and a multination system of international security to be called the United Nations.

Word help: lend or lease = loan or rent · vital = very important · arsenal = a place that makes and stores weapons · Churchill = the leader of Great Britain · self-determination = people choosing their own government · tyranny = cruel rule

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 24, “From Isolationism to Intervention” (The Lend-Lease Act (1941); The Atlantic Charter (1941)) (p. 1061).

Source GThe Four Freedoms (Primary Source)

President Roosevelt gave this speech to Congress on January 6, 1941, before the United States was in the war. He explained what the world was fighting for.

“In the future days, which we seek to make secure, we look forward to a world founded upon four essential human freedoms.
The first is freedom of speech and expression—everywhere in the world.
The second is freedom of every person to worship God in his own way—everywhere in the world.
The third is freedom from want—which, translated into world terms, means economic understandings which will secure to every nation a healthy peacetime life for its inhabitants—everywhere in the world.
The fourth is freedom from fear—which, translated into world terms, means a world-wide reduction of armaments to such a point and in such a thorough fashion that no nation will be in a position to commit an act of physical aggression against any neighbor—anywhere in the world.”

Word help: essential = most needed · worship = practice your religion · want = being poor and needy · inhabitants = people who live there · armaments = weapons · aggression = attacking others

Franklin D. Roosevelt, Annual Message to Congress on the “Four Essential Human Freedoms,” January 6, 1941. In Norton, Ch. 24, “From Isolationism to Intervention,” Comparing Perspectives: “The United States and Global War” (p. 1062).

Source G. List the four freedoms in your own words.

Point of view. Roosevelt gave this speech while many Americans still wanted to stay out of the war. Why would he describe the war as a fight for freedom “everywhere in the world”?

Reading HPearl Harbor

Early on Sunday morning, December 7, 1941, some 350 Japanese warplanes attacked the unsuspecting U.S. fleet at Pearl Harbor, on the island of Oahu. All eight battleships moored there were sunk or disabled, along with eleven other ships and 180 U.S. warplanes. The raid, which lasted less than two hours, killed more than 2,400 civilians and servicemen (mostly sailors), and wounded nearly 1,200 more.

In a larger sense, the attack on Pearl Harbor was a spectacular miscalculation, for it destroyed the American isolationist movement. . . . At half past noon on December 8, 60 million people listened on the radio as President Roosevelt delivered his war message to Congress . . . He asked Congress to declare a “state of war.” Congress approved the war resolution within minutes.

Three days later, on December 11, Germany and Italy declared war . . . The separate wars in Asia, Europe, and North Africa had now become one global conflict.

Word help: unsuspecting = not expecting it · fleet = a group of navy ships · moored = tied up in the harbor · miscalculation = a big mistake in planning · resolution = an official decision · global = worldwide

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 24, “From Isolationism to Intervention” (The Attack on Pearl Harbor (1941); America Declares War) (p. 1067).

Part 3 of 6

The Home Front

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 3: Analyze the effects of World War II on American civilians.

IN MY WORDS: Name one group whose life got better during the war and one group that was treated unfairly.

Reading IJobs, Factories, and Women

By the end of 1942, however, U.S. war production had doubled the combined output of Germany, Japan, and Italy . . . For most civilians, especially those who had lost their jobs and homes in the Depression, the war spelled a better life. Some 24 million Americans moved during the war to take advantage of new job opportunities in different parts of the country.

The war marked a watershed in the status of women. Nearly 350,000 women served in all branches of the armed forces.

More than 6 million women entered the civilian workforce during the war, an increase of more than 50 percent overall (110 percent in manufacturing alone). To help recruit women, the government launched a promotional campaign featuring the story of “Rosie the Riveter,”

Word help: war production = making weapons and supplies · combined output = everything made by all three together · civilians = people not in the military · watershed = a turning point · workforce = all the people with jobs · recruit = get people to join

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 24, “Mobilization at Home” (Arsenal of Democracy; Women during the War) (p. 1070).

Reading JAfrican Americans: Fighting Two Wars

Although Americans found themselves fighting the racial bigotry celebrated by fascism and Nazism, the war did not end racism in the United States.

In 1941, A. Philip Randolph . . . threatened to recruit 100,000 people to march on Washington to demand an end to racial discrimination in defense industries. . . . Randolph called off the demonstration in return for Roosevelt issuing an executive order requiring equal treatment in the hiring of workers.

Once in uniform, however, African Americans experienced the same kinds of prejudice they had known as civilians. . . . Stewart and the other Tuskegee Airmen flew more than 15,000 missions. After the war, their undeniable excellence helped spur military and civilian leaders to desegregate the armed forces

Word help: bigotry = hatred of people of other races or groups · discrimination = unfair treatment · defense industries = factories making war goods · executive order = a rule made by the president · Tuskegee Airmen = the first African American military pilots · desegregate = end separation by race

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 24, “Mobilization at Home” (African Americans during the War; Racial Tensions in the Military) (p. 1071).

Reading KMexican Americans: Braceros and Zoot Suits

The result was the creation in 1942 of the Emergency Farm Labor Program, soon dubbed the bracero program (for a Spanish word meaning manual laborer). Mexico agreed to provide 168,000 seasonal farmworkers, virtually all males, on year-long contracts between 1942 and 1945.

In 1943, several thousand off-duty sailors and soldiers, joined by hundreds of Whites, rampaged through Los Angeles, assaulting Latinos, African Americans, and Filipinos. Most of those arrested were not the attackers but the Hispanic victims. The weeklong violence came to be called the “Zoot Suit Riots.”

Word help: manual laborer = a worker who works with their hands · seasonal = only during part of the year · contracts = written work agreements · rampaged = attacked wildly · zoot suits = flashy clothes worn by some young Mexican American men

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 24, “Mobilization at Home” (Mexican Americans during the War) (p. 1073).

Reading LJapanese Americans: The Camps

Many of those targeted were Nisei, or second-generation Japanese Americans who had been born in the United States and thus were American citizens.

Such bigotry helps explain why the U.S. government sponsored one of the worst violations of civil liberties in American history when armed soldiers forcibly removed more than 120,000 bewildered Japanese-descended people from their homes, about 80,000 of whom were U.S. citizens. Allowed to take only what they could carry, they were loaded onto trucks, buses, and trains and transported to ten “war relocation camps” in western states.

There were no trials, no due process, no concerns about violations of civil rights. Roosevelt called the program a “military necessity,” although not a single incident of espionage involving Japanese Americans was proved.

Word help: civil liberties = basic rights like freedom and a fair trial · forcibly = by force · bewildered = confused · due process = fair legal steps before punishment · espionage = spying for an enemy

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 24, “Mobilization at Home” (Japanese Americans during the War) (p. 1075).

Picture 1Leaving for the Camps

Norton’s caption: “A FAREWELL TO CIVIL RIGHTS U.S. troops escorted Japanese Americans by gunpoint to remote war relocation camps, some of which were horse racetracks, where the stables served as housing.” (It is a primary source photo.)

What to look for: escorted = took them along · gunpoint = while holding guns · remote = far away · look at = who is in the line, what they carry, and who is guarding them

Norton, Ch. 24, “Mobilization at Home” (Japanese Americans during the War), photo caption “A Farewell to Civil Rights” (p. 1076). Primary source.

Part 4 of 6

Winning the War in Europe

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 4: Explain how the United States and its allies collaborated to win the war in Europe.

IN MY WORDS: How did the Allies work together to beat Germany?

Reading MPlanning Together

The most important development at the conference was Roosevelt’s announcement, with Churchill’s blessing, that the war would end only with the “unconditional surrender” of all enemy nations.

Late in 1943, in Tehran, Iran, Winston Churchill and Franklin Roosevelt had their first joint meeting with Joseph Stalin. Their discussions focused on the planned invasion of Nazi-controlled France and a simultaneous Russian offensive westward across eastern Europe. The three leaders agreed to create an international organization—the United Nations (UN)—to maintain peace after the war.

Word help: conference = a meeting of leaders (this one was at Casablanca in 1943) · unconditional surrender = giving up completely, with no deals · Stalin = the leader of the Soviet Union · simultaneous = at the same time · offensive = a big attack

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 24, “War Aims and Strategy” (The Casablanca Conference (1943); The Tehran Conference (1943)).

Reading ND-Day: Operation Overlord

Operation Overlord succeeded because it surprised the Germans. The Allies fooled the Nazis into believing that the invasion would come at Pas-de-Calais, on the French-Belgian border. Instead, the landings would occur along fifty miles of shoreline in northern Normandy

As the gray, misty light of dawn broke on D-day, June 6, 1944, the largest invasion fleet in history—some 5,300 Allied ships carrying 370,000 soldiers and sailors—filled the horizon off the Normandy coast.

Still, the Normandy invasion was a turning point in the war. With the beachhead secured, Allied leaders knew that final victory was a matter of time, as Hitler’s armies were caught between the Soviets advancing from the east and the Allied forces from the west and south.

Word help: Operation Overlord = the code name for the invasion of France · Normandy = a coast in northern France · invasion fleet = ships carrying an attacking army · beachhead = a safe area on an enemy beach · turning point = the moment things changed

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 24, “War Aims and Strategy” (D-Day and After) (p. 1081).

Reading OYalta and Victory

As the Allied armies converged on Berlin, Joseph Stalin hosted Franklin Roosevelt and Winston Churchill at the Yalta Conference (February 4–11, 1945) in Crimea, a Russian resort on the Black Sea. The “Big Three” agreed that once Germany surrendered, the Soviets would occupy eastern Germany; and the Americans, British, and French would control western Germany.

Churchill and Roosevelt urged Stalin to allow Poland, then occupied by the Red Army, to become a self-governing democracy. Stalin refused

May 8, V-E (Victory in Europe) day, sparked massive celebrations across the free world.

Word help: converged = came together · occupy = control with soldiers · Big Three = Roosevelt (U.S.), Churchill (Britain), and Stalin (Soviet Union) · Red Army = the Soviet army · self-governing = ruling itself

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 24, “War Aims and Strategy” (The Yalta Conference (1945); The Collapse of Nazism) (p. 1085).

Reading PThe Holocaust and the Nuremberg Trials

The end of the war in Europe revealed to the world the horrific extent of the Holocaust, Adolf Hitler’s systematic program to destroy Jews and other racial and ethnic groups that the Nazis deemed unfit to live. . . . There the Germans had imposed their “Final Solution”: the extermination of at least 6 million Jews, and many more non-Jewish peoples.

The Roosevelt administration, however, refused appeals from Jewish leaders to bomb the extermination camp at Auschwitz, Poland

On November 20, 1945, the surviving Nazi military and political leaders were indicted and forced to stand trial. . . . On October 1, 1946, the tribunal returned its verdicts. Twelve defendants were condemned to death by hanging; three were sentenced to life imprisonment; four would serve long prison terms; and three were acquitted.

Word help: systematic = carefully planned · deemed = judged · extermination = killing every one · appeals = requests · indicted = charged with a crime · tribunal = a court · acquitted = found not guilty

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 24, “War Aims and Strategy” (The Holocaust; The American Response; The Nuremberg Trials).

Part 5 of 6

The Pacific War and a New World

CORE OBJECTIVES

Core Objective 5: Describe how the Allies adapted their European strategy to fight a different enemy, under different conditions, in the Pacific.

Core Objective 6: Evaluate the efforts of President Roosevelt and the Allies to shape the postwar world.

IN MY WORDS: How was fighting Japan different from fighting Germany, and how did the war change the world?

Reading QMidway and Island-Hopping

The Japanese hit Midway hard on June 4, 1942, but at the cost of about one-third of their warplanes. American planes then struck back, sinking four of the six Japanese aircraft carriers that had launched the attack on Pearl Harbor.

The Battle of Midway was the first major defeat for the Japanese navy in 350 years and a turning point of the Pacific war.

The brutality of the fighting and the resolve of the Japanese led MacArthur and Admiral Nimitz to adopt a “leapfrogging” or “island-hopping” strategy. They liberated the most important islands and bypassed the others, leaving isolated Japanese bases to “wither on the vine,” as Nimitz put it.

Word help: aircraft carriers = huge ships that carry warplanes · resolve = strong will · MacArthur and Nimitz = the top U.S. commanders in the Pacific · liberated = freed · bypassed = went around · wither on the vine = slowly die off alone

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 24, “The Pacific War” (Coral Sea and Midway; General MacArthur’s Pacific Strategy).

MapMap 24.5: World War II in the Pacific, 1942–1945

This modern textbook map shows the land Japan controlled in 1942 (green) and the routes of the Allied attacks toward Japan (blue arrows).

Map key: Green = areas controlled by Japan, 1942 · Solid blue arrows = major Allied naval attacks · Red arrows = Japanese advances · Red star = major battle

Norton, Ch. 24, “The Pacific War,” Map 24.5, “World War II in the Pacific, 1942–1945” (p. 1092). Modern textbook map.

Map evidence. (1) Name two places marked as major battles. (2) Follow the blue arrows. In what direction did the Allies move to reach Japan? (3) Why would island-hopping make sense on a map like this?

Reading RThe Atomic Bombs

Although an intense debate emerged over the decision, Truman later explained that “we faced half a million casualties trying to take Japan by land. It was either that or the atom bomb, and I didn’t hesitate a minute, and I’ve never lost any sleep over it since.”

The bomb’s shock wave and firestorm killed some 78,000 people, including thousands of Japanese soldiers and 23 American prisoners of war. By the end of the year, the death toll would reach 140,000, as people died of injuries or radiation poisoning.

On August 9, the city of Nagasaki, a shipbuilding center, experienced the same nuclear devastation that had destroyed Hiroshima. An estimated 71,000 people were killed . . . The formal surrender ceremony occurred on an American warship in Tokyo Bay on September 2, 1945.

Word help: Truman = Harry Truman, president after Roosevelt died in 1945 · the bomb = the first atomic bomb, dropped on Hiroshima, Japan, on August 6, 1945 · casualties = soldiers killed or wounded · firestorm = a huge fire · radiation poisoning = sickness from the bomb’s invisible rays · devastation = total destruction

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 24, “The Pacific War” (The Decision to Use the Atomic Bomb; Sowing the Whirlwind) (p. 1093).

Reading SA New Age Is Born

World War II was the deadliest war in history. The Soviet Union suffered an estimated 24 million deaths, China 20 million, Germany some 8 million, and Japan nearly 3 million. The losses suffered by the United States were small by comparison: 292,000 battle deaths and 114,000 noncombat deaths.

The war transformed American life by ending the Great Depression and launching a period of unprecedented prosperity. . . . The isolationist sentiment in foreign relations that had been so powerful in the 1920s and 1930s evaporated, as the United States assumed new global security responsibilities and economic interests.

Word help: noncombat deaths = deaths not caused by fighting · unprecedented prosperity = more wealth than ever before · sentiment = feeling · evaporated = disappeared · global security = keeping the world safe

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 24, “A New Age Is Born” (Why Did the Allies Win?; The Transformation of American Life) (p. 1095).
